vignette: The typhoon hits ten years ago, faster than the weather stations can track. He and his brother Aris launch the outrigger together, chasing tuna past the reef. The radio crackles with warnings, but Aris laughs and adjusts the motor. When the waves begin to climb, he calls out. The line goes slack. They find his waterlogged jacket caught on a submerged log two weeks later, but the current keeps him. Since that day, the water has become a room he cannot enter. He still works, but only from the dock now, mending nets that smell of diesel and kelp. He tells himself it is practical, that the tiller requires steady hands he no longer trusts. When a sudden gust rattles the corrugated roof, he flinches, his shoulders locking before he can breathe. His wife, Lina, has learned to speak softly, to tap his shoulder before touching him. At night, he lies awake long after the house settles, listening to the wind push against the windows. He dreams of the engine sputtering, of the deck tilting, of his own voice cutting through the static. He wakes with his chest tight, fingers tracing the phantom weight of a rescue line that never came. The guilt sits heavy in his sternum, not as a sharp pain, but as a constant pressure, like carrying a full net for hours. He avoids the shore when the tide runs high. He tells his crew he is "tending to the gear," but really, he walks the perimeter of the pier, counting every third plank, checking the knots twice before securing them. The sea no longer feels like livelihood; it feels like a question he cannot answer. He stops going to the family gatherings by the cove. He sits at the head of the table instead, pouring tea, watching his nieces and nephews laugh, feeling a quiet distance settle in his ribs. Lina leaves his side of the bed empty during storms. He lets her. He watches the weather app on his phone, not for the boat, but for the barometric drop that always arrives before the memory surfaces. He knows the rhythm of the storm now. It matches the rhythm of his breath when he hears the first clap of thunder. He begins to doubt his own reliability, wondering if his hands are still meant for the work that shaped his father's life. He stands when the light begins to fade, folding the mended net with careful, deliberate hands. He still wears the braided thread his mother placed on his wrist the week before the typhoon, now faded to the color of weak tea. The air cools. Somewhere down the dock, a gull cries out, and his jaw tightens for exactly three seconds before he smooths his face and walks toward the house. He does not look back at the water. He knows it will return tomorrow, as it always does. He also knows he will be here, readying the same gear, the same silence, waiting for the sea to stop speaking.
